Resident core

Acute tick-borne illness

Organize the first assessment around fever with cytopenias, an inoculation ulcer or eschar, and fever with hemolysis. The resident core covers the initial decisions; detailed species, tests, and prescriptions follow in the reference section.

Companion lecture: Lyme disease. Use it for an expanding erythema migrans-like rash, bite prophylaxis, carditis, arthritis, or persistent symptoms after treatment.

Colors are specific to the selected infection, not a universal risk scale. Whole-state or country shading does not imply uniform local transmission. The maps show selected associations, not an exhaustive differential.

Static regional map and print view

Rocky Mountain spotted fever is not confined to the Rocky Mountains. Consider RMSF after compatible exposure in the central and eastern U.S., including Missouri and the Southeast, as well as western regions. Arizona and northern Mexico have important brown-dog-tick-associated foci.

Surveillance distinction: CDC geographic totals combine RMSF with other spotted fever rickettsioses (SFR). The concentration of reported SFR in south-central and southeastern states should not be presented as a map of species-confirmed RMSF. Routine serology often cannot distinguish the species. CDC geographic and vector guidance.

RegionInfections to considerUseful distinction
Northeast / mid-AtlanticLyme, B. microti babesiosis, anaplasmosis, B. miyamotoi; PowassanShared Ixodes exposure does not mean equal incidence. Hemolysis suggests Babesia; encephalitis raises Powassan.
Midwest / Great LakesThe Ixodes-associated group, with higher incidence in the upper Midwest; E. muris eauclairensis especially Minnesota/WisconsinAsk about travel to Wisconsin/Minnesota even when the patient lives in Missouri.
South-central / MissouriRMSF and other spotted fevers, ehrlichiosis, tularemia, Heartland/Bourbon, STARI; rare locally acquired divergens-like/MO-1 babesiosis; soft-tick relapsing fever in parts of TexasMissouri is not Babesia-free. Anaplasmosis reports do not by themselves establish local acquisition; serologic cross-reactions occur. Lyme requires an exposure-specific assessment.
Southeast / Gulf / AtlanticRMSF, ehrlichiosis and other spotted fevers; R. parkeri along Gulf/Atlantic areas; Heartland/Bourbon; STARIRanges overlap the Northeast and south-central areas. Eschar plus fever favors an eschar-associated rickettsiosis over classic RMSF.
West / northern PlainsColorado tick fever; soft-tick relapsing fever; tularemia and RMSF also occurMountain hiking favors Colorado tick fever; rodent-infested cabins favor relapsing fever. Southwestern brown-dog-tick settings can have severe RMSF.

Babesiosis is not exclusively B. microti, and transfusion exposure bypasses geography.

Contiguous U.S. shown for readability; Alaska and Hawaii are not assessed by this map. Geography changes pretest probability but cannot exclude infection. Ask where the exposure occurred, the habitat, season, animal contact, and transfusion history. Tick-range maps are not disease-incidence maps.

Missouri babesiosis is documented, including locally acquired divergens-like/MO-1 infection. A negative B. microti-specific PCR does not exclude other Babesia species. For hemolysis with compatible illness, request manual smear review and confirm assay coverage with microbiology. Missouri case; Missouri diagnostic guidance.

Static regional map and print view
Travel regionSelected infectionsClinical implication
Mexico / Central and South AmericaR. rickettsii spotted fever, including Brazilian spotted fever; other spotted feversRMSF also occurs in North America, including the U.S. and Canada. Exposure is focal and country lists are incomplete; the disease name is not a range boundary.
Sub-Saharan Africa / CaribbeanR. africae African tick-bite fever, especially safari/game exposures and some Caribbean islandsMultiple eschars or affected travel companions are helpful clues. CCHF also occurs in parts of Africa, but is a separate exposure and severity assessment, not a Caribbean association.
Mediterranean / Middle EastR. conorii and related spotted fevers; CCHF in selected areas, including parts of southern/eastern EuropeFever, rash, eschar can be spotted fever. Hemorrhage or severe thrombocytopenia plus relevant tick/livestock/blood exposure requires immediate CCHF precautions.
Europe / northern AsiaLyme borreliosis; focal tick-borne encephalitis (TBE); tularemia in parts of the Northern HemisphereTBE risk varies markedly within countries. Ask about forest exposure and unpasteurized dairy. European Lyme also involves B. afzelii and B. garinii.
East AsiaSFTS, chiefly China, South Korea and Japan, with human evidence also in Taiwan and parts of Southeast Asia; regional spotted fevers and scrub typhusFever, GI illness, cytopenias or organ failure after rural/outdoor exposure. Animal blood/body-fluid contact also matters. TBE occurs in parts of the broader region.
South / Southeast AsiaRegional spotted fevers; CCHF in parts of South Asia; SFTS evidence in several Southeast Asian countries; scrub typhusScrub typhus is mite-borne, not tick-borne. Eschar may be absent. Consider malaria urgently after exposure in a malaria-endemic area.
AustraliaQueensland tick typhus and Flinders Island spotted feverQueensland tick typhus favors eastern/coastal exposure; Flinders Island spotted fever principally southern Australia. Scrub typhus is a distinct mite-borne differential in tropical/northern areas.

These are selected teaching associations, not an exhaustive world distribution atlas. CCHF spans parts of Africa, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia and crosses several shaded regions. Use destination-level data before advising a traveler or excluding a diagnosis. Other zoonoses require different maps and exposure histories.

Sources [37], [38], [29], [39], [40].

Beyond the U.S., Lyme borreliosis occurs in Canada, Europe and temperate Asia. Soft-tick relapsing fever has a much broader international distribution than the U.S. cabin-associated pattern. No single regional map is an exhaustive differential. ECDC Lyme geography; Canadian Lyme geography.

Additional regional sources: UKHSA CCHF/SFTS country evidence; CDC rickettsial geography; Queensland tick typhus; Flinders Island spotted fever.

Additional geographic exceptions for the print view: scrub typhus includes East Asia and northern Australia, with human Orientia infections also described in Chile and the UAE. SFTS human evidence extends to Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam and Myanmar; Pakistan serology is a different level of evidence. CCHF extends beyond the Balkans and includes locally acquired cases in Spain and Portugal. Use the linked country guidance for dates and evidence categories.

Resident core

Start with the syndrome and the exposure

Admit or urgently escalate care for shock, hypoxemia, altered mental status, major organ dysfunction, or inability to take effective therapy. Clinical clues shift probability; no single absent rash, eschar, recalled bite, or early negative test rules out these infections. Surveillance case definitions are for reporting and should not delay bedside treatment.

Fever after plausible tick exposure with severe headache, cytopenias, hepatitis, rash, or organ dysfunction warrants prompt consideration of doxycycline. Do not wait for a rash, a recalled bite, or positive serology when RMSF or ehrlichiosis is plausible. Continue other indicated sepsis or meningitis coverage while evaluating competing diagnoses.
PatternPrioritizeImmediate distinction
Acute fever + low platelets + leukopenia + elevated aminotransferasesEhrlichiosis, anaplasmosis; Heartland/Bourbon virusHemolysis suggests Babesia. Normal counts early do not exclude rickettsial infection.
Fever + severe headache, evolving rash, hyponatremiaRMSFRash may be absent early or throughout illness. Delay in therapy can be fatal.
Ulcer or black eschar + regional lymphadenopathyTularemia; R. parkeri; travel-associated spotted feversExamine scalp, axillae, groin, and skin folds. An ulcer is not necessarily a necrotic eschar.
Expanding erythema, facial palsy, heart block, or large-joint effusionLyme diseaseLyme manifestations and treatment
Fever + hemolytic anemiaBabesiosisRequest manual blood-smear review and Babesia PCR; doxycycline does not treat it.
Relapsing febrile episodesB. miyamotoi or soft-tick relapsing feverAsk about western cabins/caves and obtain whole-blood PCR; relapses are not required.
Encephalitis or persistent febrile cytopenias despite doxycyclinePowassan or other tick-borne viruses; alternative diagnosis or coinfectionDoxycycline nonresponse is a reason to reassess, not proof of a viral illness.

Ask where and when exposure occurred, including travel, yard work, pets, hunting, animal handling, and overnight stays in rustic cabins. Record illness day, prior antibiotics, immune suppression, splenic function, pregnancy, and transfusion history. Examine all skin and lymph nodes. Initial studies usually include CBC with differential, metabolic panel and hepatic tests; add hemolysis studies, smear/PCR, ECG, lumbar puncture, or tissue sampling according to the syndrome.

Sources [1], [2], [3], [4], [5], [6].

Specimens and treatment at the first visit

PresentationObtain promptlyTreatment decision
Fever with cytopenias / hepatitisCBC/differential, renal and hepatic tests; Ehrlichia/Anaplasma whole-blood PCR, acute IgG serum; blood cultures and additional sepsis testing as indicated.Start doxycycline when rickettsial disease is plausible. Collect before therapy when practical, but do not delay treatment.

Discuss lesion swab/biopsy PCR; if tularemia is possible, alert microbiology before cultures and select ulcer material or node aspirate/biopsy. Resident core

When to perform LP and what to send

Perform LP when safe for suspected meningitis or encephalitis, including fever with meningismus, persistent unexplained altered mental status, seizures, or focal findings suggesting CNS inflammation. A tick bite or headache alone is not an indication. Assess bleeding risk, clinical stability, and whether neuroimaging is needed before LP. Do not delay empiric treatment while awaiting imaging or CSF.

Obtain opening pressure when appropriate, cell count with differential, protein, glucose with paired blood glucose, Gram stain and bacterial culture. Add HSV/VZV testing and other studies according to the syndrome, host, season, and travel; retain CSF for additional testing. Evaluate common CNS pathogens alongside tick-borne causes. Empiric doxycycline does not replace bacterial meningitis coverage or acyclovir when HSV encephalitis is suspected.

A negative standard 14-target BioFire meningitis/encephalitis panel does not exclude the tick-borne pathogens discussed here; they are not on its menu. Check the actual assay targets.

InfectionTesting or treatment decision
LymeUse serum two-tier testing. If LP is indicated, collect simultaneous CSF/serum for a validated antibody index. CSF PCR is insensitive and not recommended routinely. See Lyme CSF interpretation and sensitivity estimates.
Ehrlichia / Anaplasma / spotted feversCSF inflammation is nonspecific. Continue organism-appropriate blood, tissue, and paired serologic testing. No validated universal CSF PCR sensitivity supports exclusion; a negative result must not determine whether doxycycline is given.
Powassan / TBESerum and/or CSF IgM, with serum neutralization confirmation through public health. Flavivirus cross-reactivity requires interpretation. PCR can confirm selected early or immunocompromised cases, but negative PCR cannot exclude infection; TBE PCR is rarely positive during neurologic illness.
B. miyamotoi / other relapsing-fever BorreliaWhole-blood PCR remains useful. For suspected meningoencephalitis, discuss targeted CSF PCR with microbiology/reference laboratory. Confirm species coverage. CSF sensitivity is not sufficiently established to use a negative result as exclusion.
Heartland / BourbonTesting is primarily serum-based, selected by illness day through public-health coordination. LP is warranted by the neurologic syndrome, not by suspicion of these viruses alone. See specimens and testing access.

Sources [1], [2], [15], [16]; International Encephalitis Consortium diagnostic algorithm; CDC TBE testing; BioFire ME panel targets.

When CNS involvement changes treatment.

CNS, central nervous system; CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; HSV, herpes simplex virus; LP, lumbar puncture; PCR, polymerase chain reaction; TBE, tick-borne encephalitis; VZV, varicella-zoster virus.

Resident core

Bite-site lesions and systemic rashes

Distinguish a localized inoculation lesion from a systemic rash. An eschar is a necrotic crust over an ulcer; not every scab is an infectious eschar. Examine the scalp, axillae, groin, and skin folds. For expanding erythema and bite-reaction mimics, see Lyme rash assessment and photographs.

Eschar relationshipOrganisms / syndromesInterpretation
Common or characteristicR. parkeri, R. rickettsii subsp. californica (364D), R. africae, R. conorii; some other spotted feversAbsence does not exclude them. Multiple eschars after African safari exposure favor African tick-bite fever.
Ulcer that may be necrotic or crustedUlceroglandular tularemiaProminent regional lymphadenopathy is useful. Glandular tularemia has nodes without a visible ulcer.
Usually absentRMSF, ehrlichiosis, anaplasmosis, Lyme, babesiosis, relapsing fever, tick-borne virusesAn eschar lowers the fit for these as the sole explanation, but is not an absolute exclusion.
Important non-tick mimicsAnthrax, ecthyma, bacterial abscess, fungal infection, trauma; scrub typhus and rickettsialpoxScrub typhus is mite-borne; rickettsialpox is also mite-borne. Do not label every necrotic lesion a tick bite or spider bite.

Sources [1], [9], [10], [33].

Resident core

Initial treatment and the exceptions

For suspected RMSF, ehrlichiosis, or anaplasmosis, start doxycycline 100 mg PO/IV every 12 hours in adults. Use IV when enteral delivery is unreliable. A negative acute test does not justify withholding treatment.
ExceptionAction
BabesiosisUse atovaquone plus azithromycin, or the specified alternative combination. Assess parasitemia and organ dysfunction; doses below.
TularemiaDoxycycline is an option only for selected nonsevere promptly treated illness. Avoid monotherapy with severe infection or treatment delay >2 weeks. See the tularemia section.
Tick-borne virusesSupportive treatment; antibiotics do not treat the virus. Continue bacterial coverage only while a treatable bacterial diagnosis remains plausible.
Lyme with neurologic or cardiac diseaseRoute and duration depend on the manifestation. See Lyme treatment pathways.
Pregnancy, child, or doxycycline allergyChildren still receive doxycycline for suspected rickettsial disease. Pregnancy or allergy requires pathogen-specific assessment, not automatic substitution with a beta-lactam.

Full regimen, dose, and duration table

Sources [6], [12], [18], [19], [21], [22], [23].

General antibiotic selection, coverage and monitoring

Resident core

Tularemia with or without an ulcer

A visible ulcer with regional lymphadenopathy is suggestive, but glandular tularemia may have no ulcer. Ask about animal handling, deer flies, aerosols, and water as well as ticks. Pneumonic and typhoidal disease need not have a skin lesion.

Warn the laboratory before obtaining cultures. Select specimens by the involved site: ulcer material, lymph node aspirate or biopsy, blood, or respiratory material. Discuss PCR availability and transport requirements with microbiology. Early negative serology does not exclude infection; obtain a convalescent specimen.

For severe infection, consider an initial aminoglycoside; a second active class may be used although the benefit of combination therapy is uncertain. With a treatment delay longer than two weeks, avoid doxycycline monotherapy. Regimens and doses.

Persistent fever or enlarging/fluctuant nodes warrants reassessment for suppuration, inadequate therapy, and another diagnosis. Consider aspiration or drainage when clinically indicated. A slowly resolving node or persistent antibody alone does not establish relapse or justify indefinite antibiotics.

Sources [3], [14], [21], [25].

Resident core

Persistent fever on doxycycline

Question at 48-72 hoursNext step
Has the drug been delivered and absorbed?Review doses, vomiting, enteral access, missed doses, and interacting supplements/antacids. Use IV if needed.
Is a second or different infection present?With hemolysis, test for Babesia. With ulcer/nodes, reassess for tularemia. With cytopenias and little response, consider Heartland/Bourbon alongside other diagnoses.
Is there organ injury or a complication?Reassess respiratory, renal, neurologic, and hemodynamic status. Severe injury can resolve slowly despite appropriate therapy.
Was the initial diagnosis wrong?Revisit non-tick sepsis, viral illness, hematologic disease, and noninfectious causes. A longer doxycycline course is not a diagnostic test.

Clinical improvement is often rapid in uncomplicated ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis, but this reassessment interval is not an exclusion rule. Do not stop effective treatment solely because fever persists.

Sources [5], [6], [18], [19], [23].

Heartland and Bourbon testing does not require a failed doxycycline course when exposure and cytopenias already meet criteria. See risk factors, testing eligibility, and send-out instructions.

For prolonged unexplained fever after reassessment of the acute illness, see the FUO evaluation.

Resident core

Follow-up, complications, and prevention

For a well patient after an Ixodes bite, use the separate Lyme prophylaxis criteria. The 36-hour threshold is not a safe exclusion rule for all tick-borne infections.

ConditionComplications and follow-up priorities
RMSF / ehrlichiosis / anaplasmosisUntreated disease may cause shock, respiratory failure, kidney injury, encephalitis, or coagulopathy. Severe RMSF can cause ischemic necrosis and permanent deficits. Ehrlichiosis may trigger HLH. Follow organ function and counts; persistent antibodies do not require retreatment.
TularemiaSuppurative nodes, pneumonia, systemic infection, and relapse after inadequate treatment. Persistent enlarging/fluctuant nodes need reassessment for aspiration/drainage and alternative diagnoses, not automatic indefinite antibiotics.
BabesiosisSevere hemolysis, renal/pulmonary compromise, splenic rupture, relapse in immunocompromised hosts. Consider exchange transfusion for parasitemia >10% or severe hemolysis/organ compromise, with ID and transfusion medicine; the decision is not percentage alone.
Powassan / relapsing feverPowassan neuroinvasive disease can cause lasting neurologic deficits or death. Relapsing fever may cause hemodynamic instability, neurologic disease, and pregnancy complications; treatment can precipitate Jarisch-Herxheimer reactions.

HLH, hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis; ID, infectious diseases.

Remove ticks promptly with fine-tipped tweezers near the skin; do not burn or smother them. Use EPA-registered repellent and permethrin-treated clothing, inspect skin after exposure, and give return precautions for fever, expanding rash, eschar, dyspnea, syncope, or neurologic symptoms. Do not order Lyme serology or pathogen testing of the tick to decide treatment in an asymptomatic person.

Sources [1], [4], [8], [12], [24], [25].

Resident core

Memory aids

Recall aidWhat to rememberLimit
Babesia: BB gets AA; alternative CQBabesia blood infection: atovaquone + azithromycin; alternatively clindamycin + quinine.AA is preferred for most patients. Use CQ rather than CC so quinine is named accurately. Neither regimen is doxycycline.
E/A: two cell lines down, liver enzymes upEhrlichia/Anaplasma commonly cause leukopenia, thrombocytopenia and elevated aminotransferases.Heartland/Bourbon can look the same. Normal early counts do not exclude bacterial infection.
Babesia breaks red cellsHemolysis, anemia, bilirubin/LDH elevation, sometimes parasites on smear.A single negative smear does not exclude low parasitemia; use repeat smear/PCR when indicated.
Eschar plus nodes: sample the skinThink eschar-associated rickettsiosis or ulceroglandular tularemia; lesion PCR can help.Tularemia can be glandular without an ulcer. Warn the lab before culture.
Powassan: think brain; Colorado: fever can come twicePowassan raises concern for neuroinvasive disease; Colorado tick fever is often biphasic.Neither pattern is required or specific. These are recall prompts, not diagnostic criteria.
RMSF: rash may show up laterStart effective treatment when the syndrome and exposure fit.Neither an absent rash nor the name Rocky Mountain should exclude RMSF.

These are teaching aids, not validated decision rules. Regimens, durations and contraindications remain in the treatment table. For Lyme, a useful duration sequence is doxycycline 10 days for erythema migrans, 14-21 days for most neurologic/carditis presentations, and 28 days for initial arthritis; drug and manifestation-specific exceptions still apply. Lyme regimens.

Sources [22], [1], [12].

Resident core

Cases for discussion

Missouri, day 4 of fever, platelets 65,000, leukopenia, AST elevation, no rash, negative Ehrlichia antibody. Wait?

No. Obtain whole-blood PCR if it will not delay therapy, start doxycycline, and arrange convalescent serology. Reassess the differential and severity; a negative early antibody is expected in some true infections.

Ozark exposure, inoculation ulcer, bulky nodes, three weeks of illness. Five days of doxycycline for a presumed tick infection did not resolve it.

Consider tularemia. Warn microbiology, sample an appropriate lesion/node, and send serology/PCR. Avoid doxycycline monotherapy with this treatment delay; select an active bactericidal option and assess for suppurative nodes.

Nantucket exposure, treated erythema migrans, fever persists on doxycycline with falling hemoglobin and rising bilirubin.

Look for babesiosis with smear and PCR, assess parasitemia and organ injury, and treat with a Babesia regimen if confirmed or strongly suspected in severe disease.

Fellow detail / Reference

Diagnostic tests and timing

For Lyme serology, including stage-specific sensitivity and cross-reactivity, see the Lyme testing section.

Suspected infectionUseful test / timingLimitations and cross-reactivity
Ehrlichia / AnaplasmaEDTA whole-blood PCR during first week, ideally before doxycycline; paired IgG IFA, acute and 2-10 weeks laterPCR sensitivity falls after treatment, often within 48 hours. Negative PCR does not exclude. A fourfold IgG rise supports recent infection. Cross-reactions occur between genera and species; IgM is unreliable.
Spotted fever rickettsiosisPaired IgG IFA, acute and 2-10 weeks later; lesion swab or biopsy PCR when an eschar is present; rash biopsy PCR/IHC where availableBlood PCR is relatively insensitive in RMSF, especially early. SFG antibodies often cannot distinguish R. rickettsii from other species. One positive "RMSF" titer is not species confirmation or proof of active disease.
TularemiaAlert lab before cultures. Send ulcer material, node aspirate/biopsy, blood, or respiratory specimen as clinically appropriate; PCR through capable labs; paired serologyAntibodies often appear only after 2-3 weeks. Obtain acute serum and repeat 2-3 weeks later. Cross-reactions include Brucella. Culture poses a laboratory-acquisition risk; do not submit without warning.
BabesiaManual thin smear with parasitemia percentage; PCR if smear negative or species confirmation neededRepeat smear/PCR when suspicion remains high. A B. microti-only assay can miss other species. Antibody alone does not establish current infection; does not reliably measure clearance.
Relapsing feverWhole-blood PCR, preferably during fever before therapy; smear particularly useful for soft-tick diseaseConfirm assay coverage of B. miyamotoi versus soft-tick species. Serology becomes more useful after about 14 days; some assays cannot distinguish relapsing-fever species and may produce misleading Lyme reactivity.
PowassanSerum/CSF IgM with serum neutralization confirmation; molecular testing in selected early or immunocompromised casesFlavivirus antibody cross-reactivity complicates interpretation; contact public health. Negative PCR does not exclude.
Heartland / BourbonCoordinate with public health: serum RT-PCR plus antibody testing before day 14; antibody testing from day 14 onward, with later PCR considered in immunocompromised patients. Heartland tests include IgM and neutralization; Bourbon has no specific IgM assay, so serologic diagnosis needs paired samples.Routine commercial tick panels often omit these. Use the laboratory's specimen and timing requirements; do not assume CDC testing is available without checking.

CSF, cerebrospinal fluid; EDTA, ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid; EIA, enzyme immunoassay; EBV, Epstein-Barr virus; FDA, Food and Drug Administration; IFA, indirect fluorescent antibody; IgG/IgM, immunoglobulin G/M; IHC, immunohistochemistry; SFG, spotted fever group.

Sources [4], [5], [7], [8], [11], [13], [14], [15], [16], [17].

Fellow detail / Reference

When doxycycline is sufficient, and when it is not

Adult doses below assume usual organ function unless otherwise specified. Choose PO when absorption and adherence are reliable; use IV for critical illness, vomiting, or unreliable enteral delivery. Renal dosing is needed for several alternatives. Doxycycline generally does not require renal adjustment. Separate it from iron, calcium supplements, and antacids; take with water and remain upright. Review fluoroquinolone tendon, neurologic, QT, and aortic risks, and gentamicin renal/ototoxicity risks when choosing alternatives.

SyndromeAdult regimenReason to differ from doxycycline
RMSF or other spotted feverDoxycycline 100 mg PO/IV every 12 hours; usually at least 5-7 days and at least 3 days after fever resolves, with clinical improvementDoxycycline is preferred, including in children. Beta-lactams do not substitute. Severe allergy requires specialist management, sometimes desensitization. Chloramphenicol has worse observed outcomes and does not cover ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis; it is not a routine substitute.
EhrlichiosisDoxycycline 100 mg PO/IV every 12 hours; at least 5-7 days and until afebrile for 72 hours with improvementNo equally reliable routine substitute. Complicated disease may require a longer course.
AnaplasmosisDoxycycline 100 mg PO/IV every 12 hours for 10-14 daysDuration also covers possible concurrent Borrelia. Rifampin 300 mg PO twice daily for 7-10 days is a limited-evidence alternative for selected mild cases, such as pregnancy, after excluding RMSF and addressing Lyme coinfection.
Tularemia, nonsevere and promptly treatedCiprofloxacin 750 mg PO every 12 hours or 400 mg IV every 8 hours for 10 days; OR levofloxacin 750 mg PO/IV daily for 10 days; OR doxycycline 200 mg loading dose then 100 mg PO/IV every 12 hours for 14-21 daysFluoroquinolones provide a shorter course; consider adverse effects and interactions. Avoid doxycycline monotherapy if severe or treatment delay >2 weeks.
Tularemia, severeConsider initial gentamicin 6 mg/kg IV/IM every 24 hours for 10 days, individualized by renal function and levels; a second active class may be usedMonitor renal function and drug levels; extend interval when required. Combination benefit is uncertain. Persistent fever, abscess, or other complicated disease may require longer treatment/source control. See the neuroinvasive combination regimen and duration.
Babesiosis, symptomatic, immunocompetentAtovaquone 750 mg PO twice daily with fatty food PLUS azithromycin 500 mg PO day 1 then 250 mg daily, total 7-10 daysBabesia is a protozoan; doxycycline is ineffective. Severe disease generally uses atovaquone plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily initially.
Babesiosis, alternative regimenClindamycin 600 mg PO every 8 hours PLUS quinine sulfate 650 mg PO every 8 hours for 7-10 days; severe disease uses clindamycin 600 mg IV every 6 hours initiallyMore toxicity than atovaquone/azithromycin. Often preferred in pregnancy; individualize with specialist input. Quinine and clindamycin must be combined.
Hard-tick relapsing feverDoxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily for 14 days; amoxicillin is an alternativeSevere illness/meningoencephalitis favors initial IV ceftriaxone. Evidence is from case series, not randomized treatment trials.
Soft-tick relapsing feverDoxycycline 100 mg PO/IV every 12 hours for 10 daysPregnancy or neurologic disease favors an initial parenteral beta-lactam, e.g., ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily, for 10-14 days. Observe first 4 hours for Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction.
Powassan, Heartland, Bourbon, Colorado tick feverSupportive care; no established pathogen-specific antiviral treatmentAntibiotics do not treat the virus. Stop empiric antibacterial therapy when the evaluation adequately excludes a treatable bacterial coinfection.

IM, intramuscular; IV, intravenous; PO, oral.

Children with suspected RMSF/ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis should receive doxycycline promptly: 2.2 mg/kg per dose every 12 hours, maximum 100 mg per dose. Short courses have not been shown to stain permanent teeth. Pregnancy does not justify delaying effective therapy for life-threatening rickettsial disease. Discuss maternal/fetal risk and alternatives for the specific pathogen; rifampin is not a general replacement for doxycycline.

Sources [6], [7], [8], [18], [19], [20], [21], [22], [23].

Fellow detail / Reference

Treatment with CNS involvement

Abnormal CSF does not mandate one antibiotic or route for every tick-borne infection. These adult regimens assume usual organ function.

InfectionTesting or treatment decision
Lyme meningitis / radiculoneuritisDoxycycline 100 mg PO twice daily or ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily for 14-21 days. Oral therapy is appropriate when tolerated and other CNS infections have been addressed. Parenchymal encephalitis/myelitis requires IV therapy. See Lyme neurologic treatment.
RMSF / ehrlichiosis; suspected anaplasmosisDoxycycline remains first-line, 100 mg every 12 hours. Use IV for critical illness, obtundation, vomiting, or unreliable absorption. Do not substitute ceftriaxone because CSF is abnormal. Follow organism-specific duration and clinical recovery; severe/complicated disease may need longer treatment. CNS disease is unusual in anaplasmosis and warrants a search for coinfection or another cause.
Neuroinvasive tularemiaGentamicin plus ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin. Adult starting doses are gentamicin 6 mg/kg IV every 24 hours, individualized by renal function and levels, plus ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV every 8 hours or levofloxacin 750 mg IV daily. CDC recommends at least 10 days of aminoglycoside treatment; after stopping gentamicin and transitioning to an active oral agent, complete 21 total days. Gentamicin plus doxycycline is an alternative if fluoroquinolones cannot be used. Evidence is limited to rare cases; monitor renal function and drug levels. Routine ceftriaxone meningitis therapy is not a tularemia regimen.
Soft-tick relapsing fever with neurologic diseaseInitial parenteral beta-lactam, such as ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily; treat for 10-14 days. Observe for Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction after the first dose.
B. miyamotoi meningoencephalitisInitial IV ceftriaxone is appropriate. CDC does not specify a validated CNS-specific duration; individualize with specialist input rather than presenting the usual 14-day oral regimen as established for CNS disease. No randomized treatment trials.
Powassan / TBE and other tick-borne viral diseaseSupportive care. Neuroinvasive disease requires monitoring for seizures, raised intracranial pressure, and loss of airway protection. No established specific antiviral for Powassan or TBE. Acyclovir treats possible HSV, not these viruses; discontinue only when the competing diagnosis has been adequately assessed.

Sources [1], [7], [8], [25]; CDC neurologic Lyme regimens; CDC Powassan treatment; CDC TBE treatment.

Fellow detail / Reference

Tick-borne viruses and send-out testing

Doxycycline does not treat these viruses, but suspected viral disease does not justify delaying treatment for plausible RMSF/ehrlichiosis or other urgent bacterial disease. Supportive care includes monitoring for shock, respiratory failure, encephalitis, and other organ injury. There is no established pathogen-specific antiviral therapy for these four U.S. infections.

VirusExposure / riskWhen to consider itTesting
HeartlandLone star tick exposure in eastern, southeastern or south-central U.S., including Missouri; often warm-season outdoor exposure. Immunocompromise and multiple comorbidities have been associated with severe or fatal illness.Ehrlichiosis-like fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, GI symptoms and transaminase elevation. Persistent illness despite doxycycline is a clue; HLH or multiorgan failure can occur.Acute serum RT-PCR and serology through public health. Mayo HRTVS offers serum RNA PCR; a negative result, especially later in illness, does not exclude infection.
BourbonRare recognized U.S. infections, associated with tick exposure. Geographic limits and predictors of severity are not well established; do not restrict testing to Kansas.Fever, fatigue, GI symptoms, leukopenia/thrombocytopenia, sometimes maculopapular rash. Severe and fatal cases reported; findings overlap with ehrlichiosis and Heartland.Public-health RT-PCR and neutralization testing. No specific IgM assay; paired sera are needed for serologic evidence of acute infection.
PowassanEspecially Northeast/Great Lakes Ixodes exposure. Older adults, children and immunocompromised people have greater risk of neuroinvasive disease.Consider with meningitis/encephalitis or compatible acute febrile illness after exposure. Incubation 1-5 weeks. About 10% of neuroinvasive cases are fatal; about half of survivors have neurologic sequelae.Serum/CSF IgM, with serum neutralization confirmation through state/public-health laboratories. Consider molecular testing early or with immunocompromise; negative PCR does not exclude.
Colorado tick feverWestern U.S. and western Canadian mountain habitat, typically 4,000-10,000 feet; D. andersoni exposure. The 2013-2022 U.S. series identified likely acquisition in Montana, Wyoming, Oregon, Colorado, Utah and Idaho; not an exhaustive range.Often biphasic fever with leukopenia and thrombocytopenia. Usually self-limited; rare severe neurologic disease, particularly in children.Serum RT-PCR is most useful early. Antibody response may be delayed 14-21 days. Coordinate commercial/reference or public-health testing. Avoid blood/bone-marrow donation for six months after infection.

Sources [36], [27], [24], [15], [28], [41].

Heartland and Bourbon testing eligibility

CDC guidance uses acute febrile illness within the past three months, plus at least one exposure criterion and one clinical criterion. Exposure criteria are tick exposure in the three weeks before onset during spring through fall, or residence/travel in an area with previous virus evidence. Clinical criteria are unexplained WBC <4,500/microliter or platelets <150,000/microliter, or lack of response to appropriate treatment for suspected tick-borne disease. Treatment failure is not required when exposure and cytopenias already fit.

Before day 14, send serum for RT-PCR and antibody testing. From day 14 onward, prioritize antibody testing; later RT-PCR may still be useful in immunocompromised patients. Arrange a convalescent sample when required. CDC guidance does not accept specimens collected more than three months after symptom onset for this pathway.

Sources [16].

Where to send specimens

Contact hospital microbiology and the state/local health department before shipping. They should confirm current assay availability, specimen type/volume, storage, paired-sample timing, and the receiving laboratory. For CDC referrals, submit through the health department with the CDC 50.34 form, onset and collection dates, immune status, exposure location, and travel history. CDC pages currently caution that some assays may be unavailable; a published test menu is not a guarantee of acceptance.

In Missouri, contact DHSS communicable disease staff at 573-751-6113 during business hours; urgent after-hours disease reporting is 800-392-0272. These are public-health coordination contacts, not a verified BJC laboratory order code.

Mayo HRTVS is a reference-laboratory Heartland serum PCR option. Its catalog specifies 0.5 mL serum, centrifuged and aliquoted into a sterile container within two hours. Confirm current handling instructions with microbiology. Mayo cautions that molecular testing may be negative after more than one week of symptoms. This assay does not test for Bourbon and does not replace paired serology when indicated. CDC statements that no commercial Heartland assay exists conflict with this current catalog; verify the actual performing laboratory rather than repeating that blanket statement.

Sources [42], [26].

Imported viral infections

InfectionExposure / presentationTesting and immediate action
TBEFocal European/Asian forest exposure; occasionally unpasteurized dairy. Febrile illness may progress to meningitis/encephalitis.Consult public health for serum/CSF antibody testing and interpretation of flavivirus cross-reactivity. Supportive care; pretravel vaccination is available for appropriate risk itineraries.
CCHFRelevant travel plus tick, livestock/slaughter, or infected blood/body-fluid exposure; severe fever, cytopenias, bleeding or organ failure.Immediately involve infection prevention and public health. Arrange isolation/PPE and specialized testing before routine specimen handling or transport. Do not wait for hemorrhage if the exposure and syndrome are concerning.
SFTSEast and Southeast Asian exposure, including rural/outdoor activity or infected animal/body-fluid contact; fever, GI symptoms and cytopenias. Use the world map evidence categories rather than limiting consideration to China/Japan/Korea.Consult public health for reference-laboratory RT-PCR on acute specimens; paired serology may assist. Alert infection prevention because blood/body-fluid transmission is documented. Treatment requires specialist and destination-specific guidance.

Sources [29], [39], [40].

Fellow detail / Reference

Diagnostic performance and difficult interpretations

Test / questionEvidence and interpretation
Rickettsial PCR / IFA performanceNo universal sensitivity applies across organism, specimen, illness day, and antibiotic exposure. Tissue or eschar PCR may outperform blood for spotted fevers; whole blood is preferred for Ehrlichia/Anaplasma. An analytically specific PCR still has limited clinical sensitivity if the organism is absent from that specimen. A fourfold rise in paired spotted-fever IgG supports recent infection but usually does not identify the species.
Broad tick panelsRead targets and specimen requirements. A negative panel does not exclude pathogens not included, early antibody-negative disease, or infection suppressed by antibiotics. Multiple positive serologies may represent cross-reactivity rather than multiple active infections.

Order add-on testing through microbiology rather than assuming all PCR panels are interchangeable. Mayo HRTVS is an example of a reference-laboratory Heartland RNA assay using serum. Verify local availability, ordering, and specimen routing before collection. For unusual viruses, coordinate testing and current availability with the state health department.

Sources [1], [5], [11], [13], [15], [16], [17], [26].

Fellow detail / Reference

Coinfection, immune suppression, travel, and mimics

Shared Ixodes exposure can produce more than one infection. See coinfection in the Lyme presentation.

SituationClinical consequence
Ixodes exposure with Lyme plus persistent fever/cytopeniasConsider Anaplasma and Babesia. Doxycycline covers the former; add a Babesia regimen when infection is established or strongly suspected in a severe compatible presentation. Hemolysis is particularly useful.
Highly immunocompromised babesiosis, particularly B-cell depletionTreatment commonly requires at least six weeks, including two final weeks with negative blood smears. Monitor smears through clearance; persistent symptoms despite negative smears may justify PCR. Immunocompetent recovered patients do not need serial PCR to prove cure.
Asymptomatic Babesia detectionUsually no treatment; parasites persisting on thin blood smear for more than one month warrant treatment. Do not treat an isolated antibody alone. Individualize high-risk hosts.
Heartland or Bourbon virusCentral/southern/eastern U.S.; fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia, sometimes severe multiorgan disease. Consider after apparent ehrlichiosis fails to respond, while checking alternative diagnoses and coinfections.
Powassan virusIxodes-associated exposure especially Northeast/Great Lakes; meningitis/encephalitis. Antibody confirmation requires attention to other flavivirus exposure/vaccination.
Colorado tick feverWestern mountainous U.S.; D. andersoni; biphasic fever, leukopenia, thrombocytopenia. Early RT-PCR is useful; later serology may be needed. Supportive care.
African tick-bite fever, R. africaeSub-Saharan Africa/Caribbean exposure; multiple eschars, regional nodes, clustered illness among travelers. Doxycycline is used.
Mediterranean spotted fever, R. conorii; other imported spotted feversMediterranean/Africa and other regional exposures; fever, rash, often eschar. Some are severe. Doxycycline remains first-line; do not infer a benign course solely from an eschar.
Tick-borne encephalitis / Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic feverTravel to endemic regions of Europe/Asia for TBE; parts of Africa/Asia/Europe for CCHF. Encephalitis or hemorrhagic illness warrants urgent exposure-specific evaluation. Suspected CCHF requires immediate infection prevention/public-health involvement.
Tick paralysis / alpha-gal syndromeNoninfectious tick-associated conditions. Ascending weakness requires a thorough search for an attached tick and removal; alpha-gal causes delayed allergic reactions after mammalian products. Neither is treated with antibiotics.

CCHF, Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever; RT-PCR, reverse-transcription PCR; STARI, southern tick-associated rash illness; TBE, tick-borne encephalitis.
